story.card_text: The surgeon from the Ether Dome left Harvard his own skeleton. The man who did the ether operation and wrote the Great Elm pamphlet also started a museum: in 1847 John Collins Warren gave Harvard his personal teaching collection, and he left the school his bones too, as a lesson to 'mortality and science.' The museum's most famous object came in 1868: the skull of Phineas Gage and the iron that went through it. In September 1848, in Cavendish, Vermont, a 13-pound tamping iron shot up through Gage's cheek and out the top of his head while he was blasting rock for a railroad. He lived. The iron's engraving reportedly gives the date as September 14; most accounts say the 13th. The legend is that the accident turned a steady foreman into a drunken, aggressive wreck, and that's how he became one of psychology's founding cases. The historian Malcolm Macmillan kept digging and found something else: Gage later drove a stagecoach on a route of about a hundred miles in Chile, a job that took real social skill. Researchers now argue he made a reasonable social recovery. The weekend gallery upstairs shows the Gage case.

story.card_text: If the 1911 paper is right, this is about where Mary Dyer died. Michael Canavan, writing for the Bostonian Society, went through the diaries and the town records and argued that Boston's gallows in the 1600s stood out on the Neck, the narrow strip that carried the only road into town, just past the fortification at what was then Dover Street. His evidence piles up. In 1685 Judge Samuel Sewall wrote that a Quaker asked to put a fence around 'the ground where the hanged Quakers are buried under or near the gallows,' and that August, riding out to Dorchester, Sewall passed a few feet of ground boarded in by the Quakers. In 1699 a Quaker riding in from Braintree passed a pair of gallows on a green before he reached town. In 1703 the town asked a man to repair 'the highway beyond the gallows on the Neck.' Bonner's 1722 map prints the word 'gallows' just outside the gate. And when three people were hanged on the Common in 1789, Canavan notes, 'this time the Neck was not meant.' The plinth on Beacon Hill still says the Common.

In nineteen eleven, a historian named Michael Canavan argued that the Quakers, Mary Dyer among them, were hanged out here, not on the Common. His evidence piles up. In sixteen eighty-five, Judge Samuel Sewall wrote that a Quaker asked to fence the ground where the hanged Quakers were buried, near the gallows. That August, riding to Dorchester, Sewall passed a little patch boarded in by the Quakers. In sixteen ninety-nine, a Quaker riding in from Braintree passed a pair of gallows on a green before he reached town. In seventeen oh three, the town asked a man to repair the highway beyond the gallows on the Neck. And a map from seventeen twenty-two prints the word gallows just outside the gate. The statue on Beacon Hill still says the Common.

pitch_60: In eighteen ninety-five, the crews digging America's first subway along Boston Common dug up about nine hundred and ten people. The transit commission's annual report has a line for it. Care of human remains, two hundred and two dollars. Bad Ends is a walk through the parts of Boston history that end badly, checked against the record. A molasses tank the company painted brown so the leaks wouldn't show. A Harvard professor hanged over a debt, after the victim's dentist recognized his false teeth in a furnace. A gravestone with bullet holes, and an eighteen fifty-one book that says the bullets hit a different grave. A mummy in the room where ether surgery was first shown, whose head was once put back on with a broom handle. A monument to anesthesia that names nobody, because two men wanted the credit. Every clue walks you to the next stop, and every answer is something you read on the spot. One stop is a memorial, and it's told plainly. It starts at North Station. Bring good shoes for Copp's Hill.

seo.landing_copy:
Bad Ends is a self-guided walk through the parts of Boston history that end badly, told by someone who checked. It starts at North Station and finishes at the Public Garden, about three hours and six kilometers, with a one-hour short cut and a late walk for after dark, and it plays as a riddle hunt: each clue gets you to the next spot, and you answer by reading something that is actually there, a date on a plaque or a word on a stone.

On the way you'll stand where a molasses tank killed twenty-one people, at a burying ground where the most famous bullet story is attached to the wrong grave, outside the building where Boston's first famous painless surgery happened, in a room that now holds an Egyptian mummy, and at the corner where a Harvard professor's crime came down to a set of false teeth. You'll find out who paid for the Common's upkeep, and why that's darker than it sounds, and which gravestone people call Hester Prynne's, and what the court record actually says. You'll stand over the place a transit commission moved about nine hundred people to build the first subway in America, and it kept the receipt.

Every legend on this walk is told as a legend first, then checked against court records, city reports, inscriptions and contemporary accounts. Some hold up. Some don't. Every source is listed on the sources page.

One stop on this route marks a modern disaster with many dead. It is a memorial, not a puzzle, and it is told plainly.

Any two stops are free. Bring good shoes for two hills, and go on a weekday between nine and four if you want the burying ground gates open.

story.card_text: The company painted the tank brown, the city's archivists say, so the leaks wouldn't show. Neighbors complained they could see molasses seeping from the seams anyway. On January 15, 1919, the fifty-foot tank on this waterfront split open and put roughly 2.3 million gallons into the North End. Twenty-one people died and about 150 were hurt. The dead included two ten-year-olds, Pasquale Iantosca and Maria Distasio, and George Layhe, a firefighter at Engine 31. The company's first answer was anarchists. In April 1925, after hearings with about 3,000 witnesses, the court's auditor, Hugh W. Ogden, ruled that the owners' negligence was to blame. The physics came later. In 2016 Harvard researchers showed that the day was mild, then the temperature fell below freezing that night, and cold molasses can get four or more times thicker. Rescuers were digging people out of a substance that was setting around them. In 2019 UMass Boston archaeologists ran ground radar over the park looking for the base. They found a hard layer under the infield, then judged it most likely modern landscaping. Their best guess puts the tank about three meters northwest of where a 1917 map draws it. Nobody has dug.

story.card_text: The pockmarks in this slate are Boston's favorite bullet story. Daniel Malcom, merchant, died 1769, asked to be buried in a stone grave ten feet deep, and his stone calls him 'a true Son of Liberty' and 'an enemy to oppression.' The British put a battery on this hill in 1775, and the story goes that the soldiers used Malcom's stone for target practice. Look at it: it's pitted. The city's own sign here repeats it, and is careful to open with 'Legend states.' Now the record. In 1851 Thomas Bridgman copied and published the epitaphs on this hill. He writes that soldiers from the battery 'used some of the gravestones for targets' and wrecked others with patriotic epitaphs. But the one stone he names as 'marked by the bullets of a British foe' is Grace Berry's, wife of Thomas Berry, plot C-30; one guide dates her death to 1695. Not Malcom's. The city's burying-ground page now says only that 'many have interpreted' the scars as musket balls. So the target-practice story is in print by 1851. Which stone took it is where the story drifted toward the better epitaph. Also, it's spelled MALCOM. The city's website and Old North's own blog both add an L.

story.look_now: Look at the pocks on Malcom's stone (D-86), then hunt for Grace Berry's (C-30). Bridgman called hers 'singularly shaped.'
story.narration_script: Find the slate for Captain Daniel Malcom. He died in seventeen sixty-nine and asked to be buried ten feet down, in stone. The epitaph calls him a true son of liberty. In seventeen seventy-five the British put guns on this hill, and the story goes the soldiers used this exact stone for target practice. Look at the face. It's pitted. Great story. Now the record. In eighteen fifty-one a man named Thomas Bridgman copied the inscriptions up here and published them. He does say soldiers from the battery used some gravestones for targets. But the one stone he names as marked by British bullets belongs to a woman named Grace Berry. Not Malcom. The city's own website now just says many people have interpreted these marks as musket balls. So the target-practice story is at least as old as eighteen fifty-one. The legend just moved it to the grave with the better quote. One more thing. Read the name. It's spelled M, A, L, C, O, M. No second L.

story.card_text: In 1721 someone threw a lit grenade into Cotton Mather's house because he was pushing smallpox inoculation. He's in this vault with his father Increase and his son Samuel. Most people know him for the witch trials. Boston in 1721 knew him for something else. Smallpox came in on a ship that spring. Mather had learned about inoculation from Onesimus, a West African man he enslaved, and talked one doctor, Zabdiel Boylston, into trying it. The town lost its mind. Mather's own diary tells the next part. His nephew, the young minister of Roxbury, Thomas Walter, was staying in the house to be inoculated himself. 'Towards three a Clock in the Night,' someone threw a lit grenade, packed with powder and turpentine, through the window of the room where he lay. It hit the iron bar in the middle of the casement, the fuse was knocked out, and it never went off. The note with it read: 'Cotton Mather, You Dog, Dam you: I'l inoculate you with this, with a Pox to you.' The numbers sided with the man in the vault. More than 800 Bostonians died that epidemic. story.card_text: Dr. George Parkman was identified by his false teeth, by the dentist who made them. Harvard Medical College stood on this street, on land Parkman gave. The furnace held bone and a set of false teeth. The arms, hands and feet were never found, and the head only as fragments of skull and jaw. Nathan Cooley Keep, Parkman's dentist since 1825, recognized the set as his own 1846 work and fit it to a plaster model of Parkman's jaw. He is reported to have cried while matching them. story.card_text: The room under that dome, where ether surgery was first shown, has had an Egyptian mummy in it for well over a century. On October 16, 1846, in that operating theater, a Boston dentist named William Morton held a glass inhaler with an ether-soaked sponge to Gilbert Abbott, a young printer with a tumor on his neck. The surgeon, John Collins Warren, cut it out and told the room: 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug.' The room was an operating theater from 1821 to 1867; it's used for meetings and lectures now. Now the roommate. In 1823 a Dutch merchant, Jacob Van Lennep, brought an Egyptian mummy, Padihershef, to Boston. The city gave him to the young hospital, which charged 25 cents a look, in Boston and later Baltimore, to raise money. The story goes that he watched the ether operation. The hospital's own museum doesn't say so, and says he spent much of the late 1800s at the Museum of Fine Arts. So: maybe. In 1984, after a loan to an exhibit in Springfield, his head came loose and was put back on with a broom handle. He lies flat now, in a climate case.

story.card_text: The Cocoanut Grove nightclub stood on this block. On the night of November 28, 1942, a fire started in the basement Melody Lounge and engulfed the club in about fifteen minutes. About a thousand people were inside, in a club badly overcrowded. The main entrance was a revolving door; other exits were locked or jammed. The plaque counts more than 490 dead; the memorial committee counts 490; the Globe and others report 492. Hundreds more were injured. What followed changed how buildings are run across the country: Boston first, then other cities, tightened and enforced codes on exits, crowd capacity, door types and emergency lighting, and nightclubs were reclassified as places of assembly. The doctors and nurses who treated the burned changed burn and lung care. This plaque was made by Tony Marra, the Grove's youngest employee, who survived, and was laid in 1993 in line with the old revolving door. In 2016 it was moved here, to the corner. The memorial committee had this lane renamed Cocoanut Grove Lane. A memorial with the names of the 490 is being built in Statler Park, a few blocks north; the committee says it will be dedicated in spring 2027.

story.narration_script: The Cocoanut Grove nightclub stood on this block. On the night of November twenty-eighth, nineteen forty-two, a fire started in the basement lounge and spread through the club in about fifteen minutes. About a thousand people were inside, far too many. The main way out was a revolving door, and other exits were locked or jammed. At least four hundred ninety people died. Some counts say four hundred ninety-two. Hundreds more were hurt. Afterward, Boston and then cities across the country tightened the rules on exits, crowd sizes, doors and emergency lighting. The doctors and nurses who treated the burned changed how burns are treated. This plaque was made by Tony Marra, the club's youngest employee, who survived. It was laid in nineteen ninety-three and moved to this corner in twenty sixteen. A memorial with the names of the dead is being built in Statler Park, a few blocks north. The committee says it will be dedicated in the spring of twenty twenty-seven. Take a moment here before you go on.

story.card_text: Boston's monument to anesthesia names no one who discovered it. This is the Ether Monument, the gift of Thomas Lee. Read the main face: it commemorates 'the discovery that the inhaling of ether causes insensibility to pain,' first proved at Mass General in October 1846. That's the operation under the Ether Dome on the Mass General campus. Now look for a name. Morton, the dentist who held the inhaler? Not here. Warren, the surgeon? Not here. By the 1860s Morton and the chemist Charles T. Jackson, who shared the ether patent, were fighting over who discovered it, and others had claims too. A history in the journal Anesthesiology says the monument 'avoided taking sides,' and credits Oliver Wendell Holmes with calling it a monument to ether, or either. The figures on top act out the Good Samaritan, with the doctor in a Moorish robe and turban, which one reading takes as another dodge: no one in Boston could claim him. The quotes are from Isaiah and Revelation: 'Neither shall there be any more pain.' The stone says it was erected in 1867; the Friends of the Public Garden and the anesthesia histories date it to 1868. It's the one monument on this walk to something that stopped people suffering.
story.headline: Boston built a monument to anesthesia and left every name off it.
story.look_now: Walk all the way around it and check every face for a name.
story.narration_script: This tall granite fountain is the Ether Monument. Read the main face. It honors the discovery that breathing ether makes you feel no pain, first proved at Mass General in October eighteen forty-six. That's the operation under the Ether Dome at Mass General. Now look for a name. The dentist who held the inhaler? Not here. The surgeon? Not here. By the time this went up, the dentist and a chemist who shared the patent were fighting over who discovered it. The monument stays out of it. Oliver Wendell Holmes supposedly called it a monument to ether, or either. The doctor on top is dressed like a Moor, which some people read as one more dodge. Nobody local gets the credit. The Bible quote says: neither shall there be any more pain. After a walk full of hangings, bodies, and fires, it's the one monument out here to something that made people suffer less.
